variants.name: AbortController and AbortSignal
variants.implementation_notes: The JavaScript platform supplies the token as AbortSignal, created by an AbortController: pass { signal } into every API that accepts it (fetch, streams, timers, event listeners via { signal }), and check signal.aborted or call signal.throwIfAborted() at safe points in your own loops. abort(reason) only notifies - nothing is killed - so a signal that is never observed changes nothing, and since Node 17.2 (browsers 2022) the reason is available on signal.reason. Listeners added for aborts should be one-shot, otherwise a long-lived signal accumulates handlers.
pitfalls: abort() does not stop your own code: custom loops must check signal.aborted or call throwIfAborted(), and fan-out code must forward the signal to every child call or the tree keeps running.
Listeners attached with addEventListener('abort', ...) without { once: true } leak for the life of the signal (the Node docs warn about this); prefer throwIfAborted or one-shot listeners.
AbortSignal.timeout() is one-shot and aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException reason, so code that must distinguish a timeout from a user abort has to inspect signal.reason rather than just .aborted.
Signals compose downward, not upward: aborting a child controller does not abort its parent, so controllers must be owned by the scope that decides.

variants.name: Signal composition with timeout/any and reasons
variants.implementation_notes: Modern runtimes replace hand-rolled linked tokens with signal composition: AbortSignal.any([...]) returns a signal that aborts when any input does, and AbortSignal.timeout(ms) produces a deadline signal (Node 17.3+/16.14+, and Node 20.3+/18.17+ for any()), so a component's own timeout and the caller's cancellation become one signal passed to the work. The reason travels with the abort, which makes it possible to tell a deadline from a caller abort without bookkeeping. Prefer composition over manual controller wiring, and remember that the composed signal is only useful if the work receives it.
pitfalls: AbortSignal.any keeps references to its inputs: a long-lived composed signal attached to a short-lived request can retain controllers and listeners - create it per operation.
The first input to abort wins and the reason is taken from that signal: if both a timeout and a user abort fire, the recorded reason may be the timeout, so tests must not assume which one arrived.

AbortSignal.timeout is one-shot and cannot be cancelled: if the operation finishes first the timer still exists until it fires, so short operations should rely on the composed signal being released rather than on clearing the timer.
